summary.text: Assuming either prime family finite, bound its members by M and apply the decomposition hypothesis to \(N!/6=x+y\) with \(N=M+7\). In the Sophie Germain case \(6x+1\le N\), so it divides \(N!\) and hence the prime \(6y-1=N!-(6x+1)\), forcing \(6x+1=6y-1\), impossible modulo \(6\); the twin-prime case is identical with \(x,y\) exchanged.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
\mathcal S=\{p\in\mathbb N:p\text{ is prime and }2p+1\text{ is prime}\}
\]
be the set of Sophie Germain primes, and let
\[
\mathcal T=\{p\in\mathbb N:p\text{ is prime and }p+2\text{ is prime}\}
\]
be the set of smaller members of twin-prime pairs.

For a positive integer \(n\), the number \(a(n)=A227923(n)\) is the sum, over integers \(x\) with \(1\le x<n\), of the indicator of the following condition. With \(y=n-x\),
\[
6x-1,\qquad 12x-1,\qquad 6y-1,\qquad 6y+1
\]
are all prime. Notice that
\[
12x-1=2(6x-1)+1,
\]
so the first two primality conditions say precisely that \(6x-1\) is a Sophie Germain prime. Likewise,
\[
6y+1=(6y-1)+2,
\]
so the last two conditions say that \(6y-1\) is the smaller member of a twin-prime pair.

Assume the conjectural positivity statement
\[
a(n)>0\qquad\text{for every integer }n>1.
\tag{1}
\]
We first record its immediate consequence. Since \(a(n)\) is a finite sum of terms each equal to either \(0\) or \(1\), positivity of the sum means that at least one term is \(1\). Consequently, for every \(n>1\), there exist integers \(x,y\) such that
\[
1\le x<n,\qquad y=n-x,
\tag{2}
\]
and all four numbers
\[
6x-1,\quad 12x-1,\quad 6y-1,\quad 6y+1
\tag{3}
\]
are prime. Because \(x<n\), equation (2) also gives \(y\ge1\), and \(x+y=n\).

We shall use two elementary facts. First, every finite set of nonnegative integers is bounded above. Second, if \(P\) is prime and \(d>1\) divides \(P\), then \(d=P\): the positive divisors of a prime are only \(1\) and the prime itself.

We now prove separately that each of \(\mathcal S\) and \(\mathcal T\) is infinite.

### Infinitely many Sophie Germain primes

Suppose, for contradiction, that \(\mathcal S\) is finite. Choose an integer \(M\) which bounds all its elements:
\[
p\in\mathcal S\implies p\le M.
\tag{4}
\]
Set
\[
N=M+7,
\qquad
n=\frac{N!}{6}.
\tag{5}
\]
Since \(N\ge7\), the number \(6\) divides \(N!\), so \(n\) is an integer and
\[
6n=N!.
\tag{6}
\]
Moreover, \(N!\ge7!=5040\), so (6) implies \(n\ge840>1\). We may therefore apply (1) to this \(n\). By (2)–(3), there are \(x,y\ge1\) such that
\[
x+y=n
\tag{7}
\]
and, in particular,
\[
6x-1,\quad 12x-1,\quad 6y-1
\]
are prime.

The number \(6x-1\) belongs to \(\mathcal S\), because it is prime and
\[
2(6x-1)+1=12x-1
\]
is also prime. Thus (4) gives
\[
6x-1\le M.
\tag{8}
\]
Consider the nearby integer
\[
d=6x+1.
\]
From \(x\ge1\), we have \(d\ge7\), and from (8),
\[
d=(6x-1)+2\le M+2\le M+7=N.
\tag{9}
\]
Hence \(1\le d\le N\), so \(d\) is one of the integers whose product forms \(N!\); therefore
\[
d\mid N!.
\tag{10}
\]
On the other hand, multiplying (7) by \(6\) and using (6) gives
\[
N!=6x+6y.
\tag{11}
\]
Subtracting \(d=6x+1\) from (11), we obtain
\[
N!-d=6y-1.
\tag{12}
\]
Since \(d\mid N!\) and of course \(d\mid d\), equation (12) shows that
\[
d\mid 6y-1.
\tag{13}
\]
But \(6y-1\) is prime, while \(d=6x+1\ge7>1\). By the prime-divisor fact, (13) forces
\[
6x+1=6y-1.
\tag{14}
\]
This is impossible: the left side is congruent to \(1\pmod 6\), whereas the right side is congruent to \(-1\equiv5\pmod6\). Equivalently, (14) would give \(6(y-x)=2\), which no integers \(x,y\) can satisfy. This contradiction proves that \(\mathcal S\) is infinite.

### Infinitely many twin-prime pairs

Suppose now, again for contradiction, that \(\mathcal T\) is finite. Choose an upper bound \(M\) for all its elements:
\[
p\in\mathcal T\implies p\le M.
\tag{15}
\]
As before, put
\[
N=M+7,

aqquad n=\frac{N!}{6}.
\]
(The displayed symbol “\(aqquad\)” is to be read simply as spacing: thus the definitions are \(N=M+7\) and \(n=N!/6\).) Again \(N\ge7\), so \(6\mid N!\),
\[
6n=N!,
\tag{16}
\]
and \(n>1\). Applying (1), choose \(x,y\ge1\) with
\[
x+y=n
\tag{17}
\]
and with all four numbers in (3) prime.

Now \(6y-1\) belongs to \(\mathcal T\), since both \(6y-1\) and
\[
(6y-1)+2=6y+1
\]
are prime. Therefore (15) gives
\[
6y-1\le M.
\tag{18}
\]
Set
\[
d=6y+1.
\]
Since \(y\ge1\), we have \(d\ge7\), and (18) gives
\[
d=(6y-1)+2\le M+2\le M+7=N.
\tag{19}
\]
Thus \(d\mid N!\). From (16) and (17),
\[
N!=6x+6y,
\]
and hence
\[
N!-d=(6x+6y)-(6y+1)=6x-1.
\tag{20}
\]
It follows that
\[
d=6y+1\mid 6x-1.
\tag{21}
\]
The number \(6x-1\) is prime, and \(d\ge7>1\), so the prime-divisor fact applied to (21) yields
\[
6y+1=6x-1.
\tag{22}
\]
Again this is impossible modulo \(6\): its left side is congruent to \(1\), while its right side is congruent to \(5\). This contradiction proves that \(\mathcal T\) is infinite.

Thus the assumption that \(a(n)>0\) for every integer \(n>1\) implies both that there are infinitely many Sophie Germain primes and that there are infinitely many smaller members of twin-prime pairs. Since each twin-prime pair is uniquely determined by its smaller member, there are infinitely many twin-prime pairs as well.
